resources.title: Going further

arcs.title: Introduction
arcs.focus: use the Rust toolchain and the edit-compile-test loop

arcs.title: Basic Calculator
arcs.focus: compose typed arithmetic, branching, loops, and conversions into a calculator

arcs.title: Ticket v1
arcs.focus: model a validated ticket while applying modules, ownership, borrowing, and memory layout

arcs.title: Traits
arcs.focus: express reusable behavior with traits, bounds, associated types, and standard conversion traits

arcs.title: Ticket v2
arcs.focus: strengthen the ticket model with enums, Result-based errors, packages, and dependencies

arcs.title: Ticket Management
arcs.focus: build a collection-backed ticket store with iterators, lifetimes, indexing, and maps

arcs.title: Threads
arcs.focus: make the ticket system safe under threads, channels, locks, Send, and Sync

arcs.title: Futures
arcs.focus: move the concurrent design to async functions, tasks, runtimes, and cancellation

concepts.title: Hash and equality invariant
concepts.summary: Equal keys must hash equally and key equality/hash-relevant state must remain stable while stored.

concepts.title: Rust BTreeMap ordered-map contract
concepts.summary: Prefer the standard ordered map for total-order keys, ordered iteration, and ranges while keeping key order stable in storage.

concepts.title: Finite Rust recursive type
concepts.summary: Break recursive size with pointer indirection and select Box for single ownership unless sharing is required.

concepts.title: Rust string unit
concepts.summary: Choose bytes, Unicode scalar values, or user-perceived graphemes from the problem contract before indexing or counting.

concepts.title: Manifest requirement and lock resolution
concepts.summary: Separate authored dependency ranges and package metadata from Cargo's exact resolved dependency graph.

concepts.title: Cargo build profiles
concepts.summary: Choose dev, test, release, or custom compiler settings from build purpose and measured operational needs.

concepts.title: Workspace ownership
concepts.summary: Centralize shared resolution, metadata, dependencies, lints, and profiles while keeping package boundaries explicit.

concepts.title: Evidence-based advanced feature activation
concepts.summary: Require a concrete unmet constraint, rejected safe alternatives, bounded scope, and new verification plan before advanced Rust enters a project.

concepts.title: Bounded async concurrency
concepts.summary: Limit admitted tasks or in-flight operations to a capacity justified by resources and service behavior.

concepts.title: Async cancellation
concepts.summary: Stop future progress through dropping, aborting, or cooperative notification while accounting for owned resources and side effects.

concepts.title: Selecting concurrent operations
concepts.summary: Wait on multiple futures within one task and define what happens to every non-selected branch.

concepts.title: Asynchronous streams
concepts.summary: A stream produces a sequence of values asynchronously, combining iterator-like item progression with Future-style pending and wake behavior.

concepts.title: Async suitability
concepts.summary: Choose async for many independently waiting operations, not as a default speed or parallelism switch.

concepts.title: Async task lifecycle
concepts.summary: Track spawn, scheduling, completion, panic, cancellation, and handle ownership for every task.

concepts.title: Bindings and mutability
concepts.summary: Names bind values, with mutation requiring an explicit mutable binding and type-compatible assignments.

concepts.title: Blocking boundary
concepts.summary: Keep blocking or CPU-heavy work from occupying async executor threads needed to poll unrelated tasks.

concepts.title: Rust Book orientation and source navigation
concepts.summary: Use the Book's ordered chapters, appendices, code source, and translations to locate the right authoritative explanation without treating page views as mastery.

concepts.title: Bounded synchronous channel backpressure
concepts.summary: A bounded channel makes capacity exhaustion observable by blocking or rejecting sends instead of allowing unbounded queued growth.

concepts.title: Cancellation safety
concepts.summary: Know whether an operation may be dropped at an await point and retried without losing data or violating protocol state.

concepts.title: Channel closure protocol
concepts.summary: Use endpoint drop and send/receive errors as explicit completion or abandonment signals.

concepts.title: Closure capture
concepts.summary: Infer shared, mutable, or owned environment capture from how the closure body uses values and where the closure must live.

concepts.title: Fallible versus panicking collection access
concepts.summary: Choose optional access for expected absence and indexing only when an invalid index is an invariant violation.

concepts.title: Standard collection selection
concepts.summary: Choose a standard collection from ordering, access, mutation, ownership, and text/key semantics before optimizing.

concepts.title: Concurrency and parallelism
concepts.summary: Distinguish independently progressing work from work physically executing at the same time.

concepts.title: Value-producing control flow
concepts.summary: Choose branches or repetition constructs from required behavior while accounting for expression values and termination.

concepts.title: Copy semantics
concepts.summary: Types implementing Copy duplicate their value implicitly so the source remains usable after assignment or passing.

concepts.title: Crate roots and targets
concepts.summary: Map Cargo target conventions to the root source file from which rustc builds each crate.

concepts.title: Deref targets and coercion
concepts.summary: Deref exposes a target behind a smart pointer, and deref coercion converts references at typed function and method boundaries.

concepts.title: Rust development-tool roles
concepts.summary: Rust's supplied development tools cover automatic formatting, warning fixes, linting, and IDE integration as distinct workflow roles.

concepts.title: Compiler diagnostic evidence
concepts.summary: Extract primary span, code, notes, and applicability while treating suggested edits as hypotheses to validate against intent.

concepts.title: Documentation test boundary
concepts.summary: Compile or run documentation examples so public API guidance remains executable and current.

concepts.title: Rust edition and manifest semantics
concepts.summary: A crate selects language-edition behavior with Cargo.toml while compiler releases continue to support and link crates from earlier editions.

concepts.title: Error handling boundary
concepts.summary: Handle, translate, retry, report, or terminate at the layer that owns the corresponding policy decision.

concepts.title: Error context
concepts.summary: Add the failed operation and safe identifying details while preserving the underlying cause for diagnosis.

concepts.title: Explicit error classification
concepts.summary: Match Option/Result/error-kind variants when branches require materially different behavior.

concepts.title: Error propagation
concepts.summary: Return a failure to a caller with more responsibility or context instead of handling it prematurely.

concepts.title: Error source chain
concepts.summary: Link a higher-level error to the lower-level cause that produced it for layered diagnosis.

concepts.title: Exclusive mutable borrowing
concepts.summary: Temporarily access and mutate a value through an exclusive mutable reference.

concepts.title: Executed Cargo tests
concepts.summary: Compile and run selected unit, integration, and documentation test targets.

concepts.title: Explicit Clone
concepts.summary: An explicit duplication operation that may run arbitrary code and incur nontrivial cost.

concepts.title: Failure-path fixture
concepts.summary: Construct an input or state that deterministically reaches a required error or invariant branch and asserts its observable contract.

concepts.title: Function contract
concepts.summary: Parameters and return type state the typed boundary while the body evaluates to the returned value or unit.

concepts.title: Future poll states
concepts.summary: Polling a Future yields Pending while work remains and Ready with the output after completion; a runtime later checks pending work again.

concepts.title: Getting-started chapter roadmap
concepts.summary: The opening chapter progresses from installing Rust to writing Hello, world! and then using Cargo as the package manager and build system.

concepts.title: impl Trait positions
concepts.summary: Use bounded anonymous input types for convenience or hide one concrete return type behind a trait contract.

concepts.title: Fresh independent Rust transfer
concepts.summary: Solve an unseen problem in a changed context without tutor hints or generated solution while using allowed compiler/tests/docs workflow.

concepts.title: Rust integer conversion and overflow semantics
concepts.summary: A concrete integer type fixes range and representation; arithmetic and casts follow explicit debug/release and checked, saturating, wrapping, or truncating behavior.

concepts.title: Integration test boundary
concepts.summary: Exercise a library as an external crate through its public API and realistic component collaboration.

concepts.title: Interior mutability discipline
concepts.summary: Interior-mutability types permit mutation through shared handles by enforcing aliasing rules at runtime or through synchronization.

concepts.title: Item paths
concepts.summary: Name items from a crate root or current module with crate, self, super, crate names, and identifiers.

concepts.title: Iteration ownership mode
concepts.summary: Predict whether traversal yields shared references, mutable references, or owned items and whether the collection remains usable.

concepts.title: Iterator adapters
concepts.summary: Transform, filter, combine, or bound an iterator lazily while preserving a new iterator value.

concepts.title: Iterator consumers
concepts.summary: Drive an iterator to produce a result, side effect, aggregate, search decision, or collection.

concepts.title: Keywords, reserved words, and raw identifiers
concepts.summary: Rust reserves language keywords and future words; r# raw identifiers permit otherwise-keyword names where interoperability requires them.

concepts.title: Lazy iterator evaluation
concepts.summary: Iterator values perform no element processing until a consumer drives next.

concepts.title: Explicit lifetime annotations
concepts.summary: Name reference lifetime relationships in signatures and borrowed data types when inference is insufficient or the API contract needs expression.

concepts.title: Lifetime elision
concepts.summary: Apply the defined input/output signature rules that allow common lifetime relationships to be omitted without changing their semantics.

concepts.title: Reference lifetime relationships
concepts.summary: Describe which input borrow a returned or stored reference is tied to and the overlap in which that reference may be used.

concepts.title: Compiler-ignored line comments
concepts.summary: Text from // to the end of a line documents code for readers while being ignored by the Rust compiler.

concepts.title: Lock scope and guard lifetime
concepts.summary: Hold a mutex guard only across the protected invariant transition and release it before unrelated blocking or expensive work.

concepts.title: Macro activation
concepts.summary: Use declarative or procedural code generation only when repeated syntax or compile-time derivation is clearer than ordinary functions, traits, or derives.

concepts.title: Inline, indirect, and dynamically sized representation
concepts.summary: A Rust value has a compile-time sized inline representation unless it is behind metadata-bearing indirection; owned collections keep control fields inline and elements in separate allocation.

concepts.title: Message-passing concurrency
concepts.summary: Transfer owned data and protocol events through channel endpoints instead of exposing shared mutable state.

concepts.title: Module declaration
concepts.summary: Attach an inline or conventionally located module body at one position in the crate's module tree.

concepts.title: Module tree
concepts.summary: The nested namespace and privacy structure rooted at crate, independent of how module bodies are split across files.

concepts.title: Monomorphization
concepts.summary: Compile used generic definitions into concrete type-specific code for static dispatch.

concepts.title: Move semantics
concepts.summary: Assignment, argument passing, and returning may transfer ownership and invalidate the previous place for non-Copy values.

concepts.title: Named generic relationships
concepts.summary: Use a named type parameter when multiple signature positions or bounds must refer to the same selected type.

concepts.title: OOP characteristics in idiomatic Rust
concepts.summary: Object orientation is evaluated by named characteristics, then compared with the idiomatic Rust mechanisms and trade-offs that provide similar behavior.

concepts.title: Runtime operability contract
concepts.summary: Define configuration validation, health, version/provenance, logs, startup, shutdown, recovery, and baseline observations for a release.

concepts.title: Ownership
concepts.summary: Rules that assign responsibility for a Rust value and trigger cleanup when its owner leaves scope.

concepts.title: Packages and crates
concepts.summary: Distinguish a Cargo package manifest from the library and binary compilation units it describes.

concepts.title: Panic and violated invariants
concepts.summary: Stop normal execution when the program reaches a state its valid API contract says should be impossible or unsafe to continue from.

concepts.title: Pattern grammar contexts
concepts.summary: Rust patterns appear in match arms, let and conditional bindings, loops, and callable parameters, with context-specific binding and refutability rules.

concepts.title: Public re-export
concepts.summary: Expose a reachable public item through a chosen public API path using pub use.

concepts.title: Recoverability at a boundary
concepts.summary: Decide whether a caller can respond meaningfully to a failure without violating program invariants.

concepts.title: Reference-counted shared ownership
concepts.summary: Rc shares ownership within one thread, while Weak non-owning links break ownership cycles that would otherwise leak.

concepts.title: Regression test
concepts.summary: Encode the smallest behavior that failed so the original bug would fail again if its cause returns.

concepts.title: Rust release channels and feature flags
concepts.summary: Nightly, beta, and stable carry code through the release train, while unstable feature flags remain limited to nightly experimentation.

concepts.title: Release package verification
concepts.summary: List, assemble, extract, and build the distributable package before publishing or deployment.

concepts.title: Safe abstraction over unsafe internals
concepts.summary: Use privacy and validated constructors/methods so no safe caller can violate the internal unsafe invariant.

concepts.title: Scope and drop
concepts.summary: Trace when bindings are valid and when an owned value's cleanup occurs after replacement, move, or scope exit.

concepts.title: Send and Sync thread-safety contracts
concepts.summary: Send permits ownership transfer across threads; Sync permits shared references to a type to be used across threads.

concepts.title: Shared borrowing
concepts.summary: Temporarily access a value through one or more immutable references without taking ownership.

concepts.title: Synchronized shared state
concepts.summary: Share ownership and serialize mutation when multiple threads must maintain one common invariant.

concepts.title: Spawned task ownership and Send bounds
concepts.summary: Move owned state into spawned tasks and keep non-Send values out of state held across await when required by the scheduler.

concepts.title: Bounded test evidence
concepts.summary: Interpret a test result only for the targets, inputs, environment, and assertions actually executed.

concepts.title: Focused test execution
concepts.summary: Filter one failing test and expose its output or serialize threads to shorten the observation loop without narrowing final verification.

concepts.title: Behavioral test oracle
concepts.summary: State the observable output, state transition, error, or invariant that distinguishes correct behavior from a plausible wrong result.

concepts.title: Thread lifecycle and join
concepts.summary: Retain completion handles, observe panics, and establish when parent work may safely continue or exit.

concepts.title: Thread closure ownership transfer
concepts.summary: Move captured values into spawned work when borrowed data cannot be proven to outlive the thread.

concepts.title: Toolchain resolution
concepts.summary: Determine the rustup-selected toolchain from explicit overrides, directory context, toolchain files, and defaults.

concepts.title: Trait bounds
concepts.summary: State the capabilities a generic parameter must provide so the body and callers are checked against one explicit contract.

concepts.title: Trait implementation and coherence
concepts.summary: Provide a trait's behavior for a type only where Rust's locality/coherence rules permit one unambiguous implementation.

concepts.title: Trait-object dynamic dispatch
concepts.summary: A dyn trait object combines data with runtime method dispatch when heterogeneous values share an object-safe behavior contract.

concepts.title: Type-guided interpretation
concepts.summary: A value's type determines how its memory is interpreted and which operations are valid.

concepts.title: Unit test boundary
concepts.summary: Exercise a small behavior near its implementation, including private details only when that coupling is intentional.

concepts.title: Unsafe safety obligation
concepts.summary: State each precondition, invariant, valid lifetime/layout/aliasing state, and caller/callee responsibility the type system cannot enforce.

concepts.title: use bindings
concepts.summary: Bring a reachable path into the current scope under its name or an explicit alias.

concepts.title: Visibility and privacy
concepts.summary: Control which ancestors, descendants, sibling paths, or external crates may reach an item.

concepts.title: Cargo workspace
concepts.summary: Coordinate related packages under shared resolution, lockfile, output, and inheritable workspace configuration.

outcomes.title: Read a Rust diagnostic before editing
outcomes.summary: Identify code, primary span, relevant explanation, and the contradiction in the program model.

outcomes.title: Annotate a reference relationship
outcomes.summary: Draw input/output borrow provenance and add only the lifetime parameters required to express the valid relationship.

outcomes.title: Apply a concrete integer conversion or overflow policy
outcomes.summary: Predict and implement the exact result of typed integer arithmetic or an explicit cast under the declared overflow and truncation policy.

outcomes.title: Audit an unsafe or FFI boundary
outcomes.summary: Trace every unsafe operation to its documented obligation and prove the safe wrapper preserves it for all public safe calls.

outcomes.title: Build and explain an iterator pipeline
outcomes.summary: Compose ownership-correct adapters and a consumer, predicting laziness, order, short-circuiting, and closure capture.

outcomes.title: Choose the async boundary
outcomes.summary: Select sequential, native-thread, async-task, or isolated blocking execution from workload behavior.

outcomes.title: Choose and access a standard collection
outcomes.summary: Select Vec, String/&str, or HashMap and justify access/update behavior from the task's data contract.

outcomes.title: Choose a native concurrency model
outcomes.summary: Select sequential execution, ownership transfer, message passing, or synchronized shared state from workload and invariant needs.

outcomes.title: Choose module versus crate boundary
outcomes.summary: Keep related implementation in modules unless independent build, reuse, release, or dependency needs justify a package boundary.

outcomes.title: Choose static or dynamic trait dispatch
outcomes.summary: Select generics or dyn trait objects from heterogeneity, API, code generation, and object-safety needs and explain the runtime boundary.

outcomes.title: Choose a macro form from the expansion contract
outcomes.summary: Select ordinary code, declarative macros, custom derive, attribute-like, or function-like procedural macros from required input and generated syntax.

outcomes.title: Classify a built-in Rust data type
outcomes.summary: Given a built-in Rust value or type, classify it as scalar or compound and state what information that type gives the compiler.

outcomes.title: Classify a failure path
outcomes.summary: Choose Option, Result, or panic from the caller's recovery options and the invariant being protected.

outcomes.title: Classify a keyword and use raw identifiers when required
outcomes.summary: Determine whether a word is active, reserved, or contextual and use r# only when an external or legacy name collides with a keyword.

outcomes.title: Classify a pattern occurrence by context
outcomes.summary: Given a pattern occurrence, identify its grammar context, the names it binds, and whether that context permits a refutable pattern.

outcomes.title: Classify Send and Sync behavior
outcomes.summary: Determine whether ownership or shared references may cross a thread boundary from a type's fields and invariants, without assuming Send and Sync imply each other.

outcomes.title: Compare an OOP design with an idiomatic Rust design
outcomes.summary: Given an OOP-style design and a Rust-oriented alternative, name the OOP characteristic each provides and compare representation, dispatch, invalid-state, and maintenance trade-offs.

outcomes.title: Compose and trace an asynchronous stream
outcomes.summary: Consume or combine a stream while predicting item order, completion, pending progress, and any pinning requirement.

outcomes.title: Compose multiple futures and yield cooperatively
outcomes.summary: Combine a variable number of futures while preserving type compatibility, completion behavior, and explicit opportunities for other tasks to make progress.

outcomes.title: Configure a Cargo release profile deliberately
outcomes.summary: Given a build goal, select a Cargo profile, change only the relevant compiler setting, and explain the expected build-time, runtime, or diagnostic trade-off.

outcomes.title: Design bounded async work
outcomes.summary: Define task ownership, admission limits, queue capacity, and backpressure for an asynchronous workflow.

outcomes.title: Design bounded channel behavior
outcomes.summary: Choose a finite channel capacity and define observable behavior for admission, full capacity, receive progress, and disconnection.

outcomes.title: Design an error boundary
outcomes.summary: Place handling and translation where domain or user policy is known and keep lower layers composable.

outcomes.title: Design a minimally bounded generic API
outcomes.summary: Remove real type duplication while expressing only the capabilities and type relationships the implementation needs.

outcomes.title: Design a narrow public API
outcomes.summary: Expose the smallest stable surface while keeping implementation modules and fields private.

outcomes.title: Design a smart-pointer ownership boundary
outcomes.summary: Choose Box, Rc, Weak, RefCell, or ordinary references from ownership, mutation, lifetime, and cycle requirements and explain the cleanup behavior.

outcomes.title: Design a discriminating test oracle
outcomes.summary: Translate a requirement into positive, boundary, and failure assertions at the smallest useful test layer.

outcomes.title: Design completion and communication
outcomes.summary: Define thread ownership, message/lock protocol, closure, join, panic, and disconnection behavior without assuming execution order.

outcomes.title: Implement and use a trait contract
outcomes.summary: Define behavior at the consumer boundary, implement it on valid local types, and call it through a correctly bounded API.

outcomes.title: Implement a Rust vertical slice
outcomes.summary: Take an unseen typed requirement through API/data-flow design, error behavior, tests, concurrency/resource bounds where relevant, and clean integration.

outcomes.title: Justify or reject an advanced mechanism
outcomes.summary: Compare safe/native alternatives and approve the smallest advanced boundary only from a concrete constraint and evidence plan.

outcomes.title: Model bounded domain data
outcomes.summary: Choose primitive, tuple, struct, and enum representations that make valid states and operations explicit.

outcomes.title: Navigate the pinned Rust Book deliberately
outcomes.summary: Given a learning need, choose the relevant conceptual chapter, project, appendix, translation, or source-code path and explain why it fits.

outcomes.title: Propagate with useful context
outcomes.summary: Use match/combinators/question-mark deliberately while preserving cause and adding operation-specific context once.

outcomes.title: Repair a borrow conflict at its cause
outcomes.summary: Explain overlapping uses and change ownership, borrow duration, or operation order while preserving behavior.

outcomes.title: Select control flow from data shape
outcomes.summary: Choose if, match, loop, while, or for from the data and termination contract and justify the choice.

outcomes.title: Select a Rust development tool by task
outcomes.summary: Given a formatting, warning-fix, lint, or editor-integration task, select the matching Rust development-tool role.

outcomes.title: Select and explain a crate edition
outcomes.summary: Given a crate and compatibility requirement, set or retain its Cargo.toml edition and explain the default, compiler support, and cross-edition dependency behavior relevant to the choice.

outcomes.title: Select the next getting-started step
outcomes.summary: Given an installation, first-program, or Cargo-workflow need, choose the matching step in the opening chapter.

outcomes.title: Choose ownership or borrowing at a function boundary
outcomes.summary: Select owned, shared-reference, mutable-reference, or returned ownership from the function's responsibility and caller needs.

outcomes.title: Select the smallest valid Rust quality command
outcomes.summary: Choose check, test, Clippy, or a combination from the evidence required rather than habit.

outcomes.title: Select a Rust release channel
outcomes.summary: Given a compatibility, regression-testing, or experimental-feature need, choose stable, beta, or nightly and state the feature-flag and support consequences.

outcomes.title: Structure an inspectable workspace
outcomes.summary: Create minimal package boundaries and prove membership, dependencies, features, lints, and profiles through Cargo metadata and commands.

outcomes.title: Trace Send state across an await point
outcomes.summary: Identify which values remain stored in a future across suspension and restructure scope so a spawned future satisfies its required Send bound.

outcomes.title: Trace partial effects when a future is cancelled
outcomes.summary: Determine which externally visible or caller-owned state changes survive when a pending future is dropped before completion.

outcomes.title: Trace a closure capture
outcomes.summary: Predict whether a closure borrows immutably, borrows mutably, or takes ownership of each captured value and what remains usable around the closure.

outcomes.title: Trace a deref coercion
outcomes.summary: Follow the Deref target chain used to convert one reference type into the reference type required by a concrete call.

outcomes.title: Trace expression values
outcomes.summary: Predict the type and value produced by blocks, branches, function bodies, and statement boundaries before compilation.

outcomes.title: Trace future polling and executor progress
outcomes.summary: Trace a future through Ready and Pending states and explain when the runtime advances, sleeps, or checks the future again.

outcomes.title: Trace iteration ownership
outcomes.summary: Predict Item values and post-loop availability for borrowed, mutable, and consuming collection traversal.

outcomes.title: Trace a Rust value representation boundary
outcomes.summary: Predict inline size, separate allocation, reference metadata, and Vec length/capacity behavior for a concrete type or operation.

outcomes.title: Trace a module path
outcomes.summary: Draw the crate/module tree and determine whether a concrete absolute or relative path resolves.

outcomes.title: Trace ownership and drop
outcomes.summary: Mark owner, move/copy/clone operations, valid places, and cleanup for every relevant value in a small program.

outcomes.title: Use a function pointer or returned closure boundary
outcomes.summary: Select a function pointer when a callable must be a function item and use an explicit trait-object or impl-Trait boundary when returning a closure.

outcomes.title: Distinguish installed binaries from Cargo custom commands
outcomes.summary: Determine whether a Cargo-related executable is installed from a package or discovered as a cargo-prefixed subcommand, then invoke the matching entry point.

outcomes.title: Document intent with a line comment
outcomes.summary: Place a concise // comment that explains non-obvious intent and verify that removing or changing comment text does not change execution.

outcomes.title: Verify the active Rust toolchain
outcomes.summary: Explain the winning override and record exact rustc, Cargo, and component availability before debugging version behavior.

library.title: The Rust Programming Language
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: The canonical guided tour. This curriculum follows its chapter order so every module has an authoritative long-form counterpart.

library.title: Rust by Example
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Runnable snippets for the same concepts. Use it when you want to see the shape of the code before reading the argument for it.

library.title: Rustlings
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Small compiler-error-driven fixes. Closest external analogue to this app's terminal work; good for extra repetitions.

library.title: The Rust Standard Library
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Primary API reference. Every collection, trait, and guarantee named in a lesson is specified here first.

library.title: The Rust Reference
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Language-level specification. Reach for it when you need the rule rather than an explanation of the rule.

library.title: The rustc Error Index
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: One page per E-code with a minimal reproduction and repair. The compiler-error nodes in the concept map link straight here.

library.title: The Cargo Book
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Manifest keys, profiles, workspaces, features, and publishing. The authority behind every cargo command this app runs.

library.title: The Edition Guide
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: What changed across 2015/2018/2021/2024. Read it before trusting an older blog post or Stack Overflow answer.

library.title: Comprehensive Rust
library.author: Google
library.blurb: A dense multi-day course with speaker notes, plus bare-metal, Android, and Chromium tracks the Book never covers.

library.title: The Rust Cookbook
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Task-shaped recipes using well-known crates. Useful once you know the language and need the ecosystem's default answer.

library.title: Rust Design Patterns
library.author: rust-unofficial
library.blurb: Idioms, patterns, and named anti-patterns. The vocabulary layer between 'it compiles' and 'a reviewer would accept it'.

library.title: Effective Rust
library.author: David Drysdale
library.blurb: Thirty-five specific pieces of advice on types, traits, dependencies, and tooling. Commercially published, so this app links to it and never reproduces it.

library.title: Rust API Guidelines
library.author: The Rust Library Team
library.blurb: The checklist library authors are held to: naming, interoperability, flexibility, future proofing.

library.title: The Rustonomicon
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: The dark arts of unsafe Rust: aliasing, variance, drop order, and the invariants you now have to uphold by hand.

library.title: Learn Rust With Entirely Too Many Linked Lists
library.author: Aria Beingessner
library.blurb: The best available treatment of ownership under pressure. Work it after Chapter 15; it turns smart pointers into muscle memory.

library.title: Rust Atomics and Locks
library.author: Mara Bos
library.blurb: Free online edition covering memory ordering, building your own locks, and what the OS actually does underneath.

library.title: Asynchronous Programming in Rust
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Futures, executors, pinning, and cancellation from first principles rather than from one runtime's API surface.

library.title: Tokio Tutorial
library.author: The Tokio Contributors
library.blurb: The concrete counterpart to the async book: tasks, channels, select, shared state, and graceful shutdown in a real runtime.

library.title: The Little Book of Rust Macros
library.author: Veykril (community edition)
library.blurb: macro_rules! from fragment specifiers to hygiene, then the bridge into procedural macros.

library.title: The Rust Performance Book
library.author: Nicholas Nethercote
library.blurb: Profiling first, then measured wins: allocation, hashing, bounds checks, build configuration, and benchmarking discipline.

library.title: Rust Quiz
library.author: David Tolnay
library.blurb: Short programs with surprising output and a full explanation. Excellent calibration for how well you actually read Rust.

library.title: TheAlgorithms / Rust
library.author: TheAlgorithms community
library.blurb: Reference implementations for classic algorithms in idiomatic-ish Rust. Compare against your own after you have solved a pattern.

library.title: Exercism Rust Track
library.author: Exercism
library.blurb: Around a hundred graded exercises with published community solutions — the widest source of alternative idiom for a solved problem.

library.title: Learn Rust (rust-lang.org)
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: The project's own index of official learning material. Start here to see what is canonical before trusting a third-party summary.

library.title: The rustc Book
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Compiler flags, lint levels, codegen options, and platform support. Read the lints chapter before you reach for #[allow].

library.title: The rustdoc Book
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: How doc comments, intra-doc links, and doctests work. Doctests are a second test suite most beginners never switch on.

library.title: Clippy Documentation
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Configuring and running Clippy, lint groups, and how to justify an allow. Pairs with the searchable lint list dataset below.

library.title: The Rust Style Guide
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: The formatting rules rustfmt implements, with the reasoning. Useful when a formatting choice looks arbitrary.

library.title: rustfmt Configuration
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Every rustfmt.toml option with before/after examples, filterable by stable versus unstable.

library.title: The Unstable Book
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Nightly-only features and their tracking issues. Read it to understand where the language is going, not to build on it.

library.title: The Rust RFC Book
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: The accepted design documents behind every major feature. An RFC's 'Motivation' and 'Alternatives' sections explain why a rule is the way it is.

library.title: The FLS (Rust language specification)
library.author: The Rust Project (originally Ferrous Systems and AdaCore)
library.blurb: A rigorously structured specification of Rust, maintained by the Rust project since 2025. Numbered paragraphs make it the most citable language reference.

library.title: Unsafe Code Guidelines Reference
library.author: Rust Unsafe Code Guidelines Working Group
library.blurb: Layout, validity, and aliasing rules that unsafe code must uphold. Read after the Rustonomicon when you need the precise invariant.

library.title: Rust Compiler Development Guide
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: How rustc is built: HIR, MIR, type checking, and the borrow checker. The MIR borrow-check chapter shows what 'the borrow checker' literally computes.

library.title: Rust Forge
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Release trains, team structure, and contribution process. Where to go when you want to contribute to Rust itself.

library.title: rust-analyzer Manual
library.author: rust-analyzer contributors
library.blurb: Editor setup, assists, and inlay hints. Inlay type hints are the fastest way to see what inference decided.

library.title: Miri
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: An interpreter that detects undefined behaviour in tests. Run it on any crate that contains unsafe before you believe a safety comment.

library.title: Rust Playground
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Run snippets on stable, beta, or nightly and view MIR, LLVM IR, or assembly. Also runs Clippy and Miri on a snippet.

library.title: Compiler Explorer
library.author: Matt Godbolt and contributors
library.blurb: See the machine code rustc emits side by side with source. It turns 'zero-cost abstraction' from a slogan into something you can check.

library.title: The Rust Book: Experimental Edition (Brown University)
library.author: Will Crichton, Gavin Gray, Shriram Krishnamurthi (Cognitive Engineering Lab)
library.blurb: The official Book with embedded quizzes, a redesigned ownership chapter, and 'Ownership Inventory' scenarios. Its quiz data drove published research on how people learn Rust.

library.title: Rust By Practice
library.author: sunface and contributors
library.blurb: Fill-in and fix-the-bug exercises organised by the same topics as the Book, with published solutions. Good for a second round after each chapter.

library.title: 100 Exercises to Learn Rust
library.author: Luca Palmieri (Mainmatter)
library.blurb: A test-driven course built around one ticketing domain. The app already embeds this pack as its Mainmatter practice track; the upstream site has the prose.

library.title: Easy Rust
library.author: Dave MacLeod
library.blurb: The whole language in simple English with short examples. A good second explanation when the Book's phrasing does not land.

library.title: Tour of Rust
library.author: Richard Anaya and contributors
library.blurb: Bite-sized pages each with a runnable example, translated into many languages. Fast syntax orientation before the deeper chapters.

library.title: A Gentle Introduction to Rust
library.author: Steve Donovan
library.blurb: A pragmatic tour aimed at programmers from other languages, with a candid 'pain points' chapter.

library.title: Rust for C++ Programmers
library.author: Nick Cameron
library.blurb: Maps unique_ptr, shared_ptr, and references onto Box, Rc, and borrows. Read it if you already think in C++ ownership terms.

library.title: Rust Language Cheat Sheet
library.author: Ralf Biedert
library.license: Code snippets CC0-1.0; prose free to read
library.blurb: Dense one-page reference with memory-layout diagrams for String, Vec, Box, and Rc. Keep it open while doing exercises.

library.title: Command Line Applications in Rust
library.author: Rust CLI Working Group
library.blurb: A 15-minute CLI tutorial followed by chapters on argument parsing, errors, output, and testing binaries. A natural first real project after chapter 11.

library.title: The Embedded Rust Book
library.author: Rust Embedded Working Group
library.license: Prose CC-BY-SA-4.0; code MIT OR Apache-2.0
library.blurb: no_std, peripherals as owned singletons, and interrupts. Shows ownership modelling hardware, not just memory.

library.title: Discovery (micro:bit v2)
library.author: Rust Embedded Working Group
library.license: Prose CC-BY-4.0; code MIT OR Apache-2.0
library.blurb: A beginner embedded course on an inexpensive micro:bit board, from blinking an LED to serial communication.

library.title: The Embedonomicon
library.author: Rust Embedded Working Group
library.license: Prose CC-BY-SA-4.0; code MIT OR Apache-2.0
library.blurb: Build a no_std program from nothing: linker scripts, the reset handler, and memory layout.

library.title: Writing an OS in Rust
library.author: Philipp Oppermann
library.license: Prose CC-BY-NC-4.0; code MIT OR Apache-2.0
library.blurb: A step-by-step x86_64 kernel: VGA output, interrupts, paging, heap allocation, and async tasks. The best long project for unsafe and no_std.

library.title: Rust and WebAssembly
library.author: Rust and WebAssembly Working Group (archived)
library.blurb: Game of Life compiled to WebAssembly, with profiling and size optimisation. The organisation is archived, but the model of the JS/Wasm boundary still holds.

library.title: Serde
library.author: Erick Tryzelaar, David Tolnay
library.blurb: How the de facto serialization framework uses traits and derive macros. The data-model page is a masterclass in trait design.

library.title: Criterion.rs User Guide
library.author: Brook Heisler and contributors
library.blurb: Statistics-driven benchmarking. Pair it with the Performance Book so optimisations are measured rather than guessed.

library.title: Rust Fuzz Book
library.author: rust-fuzz contributors
library.blurb: cargo-fuzz and afl.rs from first target to structure-aware fuzzing. The next step after unit and property tests.

library.title: mini-redis
library.author: Tokio contributors
library.blurb: An intentionally readable Redis server written to teach Tokio. Read it alongside the Tokio tutorial.

library.title: Procedural Macros Workshop
library.author: David Tolnay
library.blurb: Five test-driven projects that build real derive, attribute, and function-like macros. The practical sequel to the Little Book of Rust Macros.

library.title: Rust Algorithm Club
library.author: Weihang Lo and contributors
library.blurb: Classic algorithms and data structures explained with Rust implementations. Useful beside the interview-practice track.

library.title: Take your first steps with Rust (Microsoft Learn)
library.author: Microsoft
library.blurb: A free guided learning path with sandboxed exercises. Another voice for the chapter 1–11 material.

library.title: ripgrep
library.author: Andrew Gallant
library.blurb: A production command-line tool with exemplary error handling, crate boundaries, and comments. The standard recommendation for 'show me good Rust'.

library.title: uutils coreutils
library.author: uutils contributors
library.blurb: Rust rewrites of ls, cat, wc, and friends. Each utility is small enough to read in one sitting and has a known specification.

library.title: The standard library source
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Every std doc page has a 'Source' link. Reading Vec, Option, and RefCell's implementations shows small audited unsafe wrapped in safe APIs.

library.title: axum examples
library.author: Tokio contributors
library.blurb: Dozens of small, focused web-service examples (the framework this app's own service uses).

library.title: rustc UI test suite
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Thousands of small programs paired with the exact diagnostics rustc must print. The largest corpus of 'predict the compiler error' drills in existence.

library.title: rustc error-code explanations (source)
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: One Markdown file per E-code with an erroneous example and a fix: the machine-readable source behind the Error Index.

library.title: Clippy lint list
library.author: The Rust Project Developers
library.blurb: Over 800 lints, each with 'what it does', 'why is this bad', and a before/after example. Browse one category a week as an idiom curriculum.

library.title: RustSec Advisory Database
library.author: Rust Secure Code Working Group
library.blurb: Every published vulnerability in a crates.io crate. Reading the unsafe-related advisories is a catalogue of real soundness bugs.

library.title: crates.io database dump
library.author: crates.io team

modules.title: Introduction
modules.summary: Orient to the complete Rust Book, its audience, its toolchain assumptions, and the evidence-first way this track links reading to practice.

modules.title: Getting Started
modules.summary: Install the toolchain and use Cargo to create, build, run, format, and inspect a small Rust program.

modules.title: Programming a Guessing Game
modules.summary: Build a complete input loop while meeting variables, matching, error handling, crates, and generated random values in context.

modules.title: Common Programming Concepts
modules.summary: Use bindings, types, functions, expressions, and control flow while letting the type checker expose ambiguous intent.

modules.title: Understanding Ownership
modules.summary: Predict moves, copies, borrows, slices, and drop points without trial-and-error compilation.

modules.title: Using Structs to Structure Related Data
modules.summary: Model domain data with structs, methods, associated functions, and derived traits.

modules.title: Enums and Pattern Matching
modules.summary: Represent alternatives with enums and exhaustively transform them with match and if let.

modules.title: Managing Growing Projects
modules.summary: Organize crates and modules, choose visibility deliberately, and import names without hiding ownership boundaries.

modules.title: Common Collections
modules.summary: Choose vectors, strings, and hash maps, then traverse and update them without violating borrowing rules.

modules.title: Error Handling
modules.summary: Separate recoverable failures from invariant violations using Result, propagation, and deliberate panic boundaries.

modules.title: Generic Types, Traits, and Lifetimes
modules.summary: Express shared behavior with generics and traits, and use lifetimes to relate borrowed inputs and outputs.

modules.title: Writing Automated Tests
modules.summary: Write focused unit and integration tests, assert useful evidence, and control which test subsets run.

modules.title: An I/O Project: Building a Command Line Program
modules.summary: Build a minigrep-style CLI by separating argument parsing, file I/O, domain logic, and user-facing errors.

modules.title: Functional Language Features
modules.summary: Use closures and iterators to describe transformations while retaining ownership and performance control.

modules.title: More about Cargo and Crates.io
modules.summary: Tune release profiles, document public APIs, structure workspaces, and reason about publishing contracts.

modules.title: Smart Pointers
modules.summary: Use Box, Rc, RefCell, Drop, and Deref where plain ownership cannot express recursive or shared structures.

modules.title: Fearless Concurrency
modules.summary: Coordinate threads with ownership transfer, channels, mutexes, and thread-safe sharing traits.

modules.title: Async and Await
modules.summary: Compose futures, cancellation, streams, and concurrent tasks without confusing concurrency with parallelism.

modules.title: Object-Oriented Programming Features
modules.summary: Evaluate encapsulation, trait objects, and state patterns as design tools rather than language labels.

modules.title: Patterns and Matching
modules.summary: Destructure nested values with precise refutable and irrefutable patterns, guards, bindings, and ranges.

modules.title: Advanced Features
modules.summary: Use unsafe Rust, advanced traits and types, macros, and function pointers behind reviewed safe abstractions.

modules.title: Final Project: Multithreaded Web Server
modules.summary: Assemble networking, thread pools, graceful shutdown, and protocol parsing into a bounded server.

modules.title: Appendices
modules.summary: Use the Book appendices as reviewed references for language vocabulary, operators, derivable traits, tools, editions, translations, and Rust release channels.

The Rust programming language helps you write faster, more reliable software.
High-level ergonomics and low-level control are often at odds in programming
language design; Rust challenges that conflict. Through balancing powerful
technical capacity and a great developer experience, Rust gives you the option
to control low-level details (such as memory usage) without all the hassle
Rust is ideal for many people for a variety of reasons. Let’s look at a few of
Rust is proving to be a productive tool for collaborating among large teams of
developers with varying levels of systems programming knowledge. Low-level code
is prone to various subtle bugs, which in most other languages can only be
caught through extensive testing and careful code review by experienced
developers. In Rust, the compiler plays a gatekeeper role by refusing to
compile code with these elusive bugs, including concurrency bugs. By working
alongside the compiler, the team can spend its time focusing on the program’s
logic rather than chasing down bugs.
Rust also brings contemporary developer tools to the systems programming world:
Cargo, the included dependency manager and build tool, makes adding,
compiling, and managing dependencies painless and consistent across the Rust
formatting tool ensures a consistent coding style across
The Rust Language Server powers integrated development environment (IDE)
integration for code completion and inline error messages.

concepts. Using Rust, many people have learned about topics like operating
systems development. The community is very welcoming and happy to answer
students’ questions. Through efforts such as this book, the Rust teams want to
make systems concepts more accessible to more people, especially those new to
Hundreds of companies, large and small, use Rust in production for a variety of
tasks, including command line tools, web services, DevOps tooling, embedded
devices, audio and video analysis and transcoding, cryptocurrencies,
bioinformatics, search engines, Internet of Things applications, machine
learning, and even major parts of the Firefox web browser.
Rust is for people who want to build the Rust programming language, community,
developer tools, and libraries. We’d love to have you contribute to the Rust
People Who Value Speed and Stability
Rust is for people who crave speed and stability in a language. By speed, we
mean both how quickly Rust code can run and the speed at which Rust lets you
write programs. The Rust compiler’s checks ensure stability through feature
additions and refactoring. This is in contrast to the brittle legacy code in
languages without these checks, which developers are often afraid to modify. By
striving for zero-cost abstractions—higher-level features that compile to
lower-level code as fast as code written manually—Rust endeavors to make safe
code be fast code as well.
The Rust language hopes to support many other users as well; those mentioned
here are merely some of the biggest stakeholders. Overall, Rust’s greatest
ambition is to eliminate the trade-offs that programmers have accepted for
Rust a try, and see if its choices work for you.

children.text: Cargo is Rust’s build system and package manager. Most Rustaceans use this tool
to manage their Rust projects because Cargo handles a lot of tasks for you,
such as building your code, downloading the libraries your code depends on, and
building those libraries. (We call the libraries that your code needs
The simplest Rust programs, like the one we’ve written so far, don’t have any
dependencies. If we had built the “Hello, world!” project with Cargo, it would
only use the part of Cargo that handles building your code. As you write more
complex Rust programs, you’ll add dependencies, and if you start a project
using Cargo, adding dependencies will be much easier to do.
Because the vast majority of Rust projects use Cargo, the rest of this book
assumes that you’re using Cargo too. Cargo comes installed with Rust if you
used the official installers discussed in the
through some other means, check whether Cargo is installed by entering the
If you see a version number, you have it! If you see an error, such as
, look at the documentation for your method of installation to
determine how to install Cargo separately.
Let’s create a new project using Cargo and look at how it differs from our
original “Hello, world!” project. Navigate back to your
(or wherever you decided to store your code). Then, on any operating system,

your program: the name, the version, and the edition of Rust to use. We’ll talk

of your project’s dependencies. In Rust, packages of code are referred to as

first project in Chapter 2, so we’ll use this dependencies section then.
Cargo has generated a “Hello, world!” program for you, just like the one we
wrote in Listing 1-1! So far, the differences between our project and the
project Cargo generated are that Cargo placed the code in the
configuration file in the top directory.

configuration files, and anything else not related to your code. Using Cargo
helps you organize your projects. There’s a place for everything, and
If you started a project that doesn’t use Cargo, as we did with the “Hello,
world!” project, you can convert it to a project that does use Cargo. Move the

Building and Running a Cargo Project
Now let’s look at what’s different when we build and run the “Hello, world!”

$ cargo build

    Finished dev [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 2.85 secs

directory. Because the default build is a debug build, Cargo puts the binary in

We just built a project with

$ cargo run
    Finished dev [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.0 secs

Hello, world!

and then use the whole path to the binary, so most developers use
Notice that this time we didn’t see output indicating that Cargo was compiling

rebuild but just ran the binary. If you had modified your source code, Cargo
would have rebuilt the project before running it, and you would have seen this

$ cargo run
   Compiling hello_cargo v0.1.0 (file:///projects/hello_cargo)
    Finished dev [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.33 secs
     Running `target/debug/hello_cargo`
Hello, world!

your code to make sure it compiles but doesn’t produce an executable:

$ cargo check

    Finished dev [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.32 secs
Why would you not want an executable? Often,

continually checking your work while writing the code, using

An additional advantage of using Cargo is that the commands are the same no
matter which operating system you’re working on. So, at this point, we’ll no
longer provide specific instructions for Linux and macOS versus Windows.
When your project is finally ready for release, you can use

This project was a hands-on way to introduce you to many new Rust concepts:
, functions, the use of external crates, and more. In the next
few chapters, you’ll learn about these concepts in more detail. Chapter 3
covers concepts that most programming languages have, such as variables, data
types, and functions, and shows how to use them in Rust. Chapter 4 explores
ownership, a feature that makes Rust different from other languages. Chapter 5
discusses structs and method syntax, and Chapter 6 explains how enums work.

children.text: This chapter covers concepts that appear in almost every programming language
and how they work in Rust. Many programming languages have much in common at
their core. None of the concepts presented in this chapter are unique to Rust,
but we’ll discuss them in the context of Rust and explain the conventions
Specifically, you’ll learn about variables, basic types, functions, comments,
and control flow. These foundations will be in every Rust program, and learning
them early will give you a strong core to start from.
The Rust language has a set of
that are reserved for use by the
language only, much as in other languages. Keep in mind that you cannot use
these words as names of variables or functions. Most of the keywords have
special meanings, and you’ll be using them to do various tasks in your Rust
programs; a few have no current functionality associated with them but have

keyTerms.definition: _Ownership_ is a set of rules that govern how a Rust program manages memory. All programs have to manage the way they use a computer’s memory while running. Some languages have garbage collection that regularly looks for no-longer-used memory as the program runs; in other languages, the programmer must explicitly allocate and free the memory. Rust uses a third approach: Memory is managed through a system of ownership with a set of rules that the compiler checks. If any of the rules are violated, the program won’t compile. None of the features of ownership will slow down your program while it’s running.
At a program point, each value has one owner; ownership can transfer, and an owned value is dropped when its owner leaves scope unless it was moved.
A transfer of a value's ownership that makes the source place unusable unless it is reinitialized.

children.text: is a set of rules that govern how a Rust program manages memory.
All programs have to manage the way they use a computer’s memory while running.
Some languages have garbage collection that regularly looks for no-longer-used
memory as the program runs; in other languages, the programmer must explicitly
allocate and free the memory. Rust uses a third approach: Memory is managed
through a system of ownership with a set of rules that the compiler checks. If
any of the rules are violated, the program won’t compile. None of the features
of ownership will slow down your program while it’s running.
Because ownership is a new concept for many programmers, it does take some time
to get used to. The good news is that the more experienced you become with Rust
and the rules of the ownership system, the easier you’ll find it to naturally
develop code that is safe and efficient. Keep at it!
When you understand ownership, you’ll have a solid foundation for understanding
the features that make Rust unique. In this chapter, you’ll learn ownership by
working through some examples that focus on a very common data structure:
Many programming languages don’t require you to think about the stack and the
heap very often. But in a systems programming language like Rust, whether a
value is on the stack or the heap affects how the language behaves and why
you have to make certain decisions. Parts of ownership will be described in
relation to the stack and the heap later in this chapter, so here is a brief
Both the stack and the heap are parts of memory available to your code to use
at runtime, but they are structured in different ways. The stack stores
values in the order it gets them and removes the values in the opposite
order. This is referred to as
plates: When you add more plates, you put them on top of the pile, and when
you need a plate, you take one off the top. Adding or removing plates from
the middle or bottom wouldn’t work as well! Adding data is called
data stored on the stack must have a known, fixed size. Data with an unknown
size at compile time or a size that might change must be stored on the heap
The heap is less organized: When you put data on the heap, you request a
certain amount of space. The memory allocator finds an empty spot in the heap
that is big enough, marks it as being in use, and returns a

and is sometimes abbreviated as just

known, fixed size, you can store the pointer on the stack, but when you want
the actual data, you must follow the pointer. Think of being seated at a
restaurant. When you enter, you state the number of people in your group, and
the host finds an empty table that fits everyone and leads you there. If
someone in your group comes late, they can ask where you’ve been seated to
Pushing to the stack is faster than allocating on the heap because the
allocator never has to search for a place to store new data; that location is
always at the top of the stack. Comparatively, allocating space on the heap
requires more work because the allocator must first find a big enough space
to hold the data and then perform bookkeeping to prepare for the next
Accessing data in the heap is generally slower than accessing data on the
stack because you have to follow a pointer to get there. Contemporary
processors are faster if they jump around less in memory. Continuing the
analogy, consider a server at a restaurant taking orders from many tables.
It’s most efficient to get all the orders at one table before moving on to
the next table. Taking an order from table A, then an order from table B,
then one from A again, and then one from B again would be a much slower
process. By the same token, a processor can usually do its job better if it
works on data that’s close to other data (as it is on the stack) rather than
farther away (as it can be on the heap).
When your code calls a function, the values passed into the function
(including, potentially, pointers to data on the heap) and the function’s
local variables get pushed onto the stack. When the function is over, those
values get popped off the stack.
Keeping track of what parts of code are using what data on the heap,
minimizing the amount of duplicate data on the heap, and cleaning up unused
data on the heap so that you don’t run out of space are all problems that
ownership addresses. Once you understand ownership, you won’t need to think
about the stack and the heap very often. But knowing that the main purpose of
ownership is to manage heap data can help explain why it works the way it

keyTerms.definition: A _struct_, or _structure_, is a custom data type that lets you package together and name multiple related values that make up a meaningful group. If you’re familiar with an object-oriented language, a struct is like an object’s data attributes. In this chapter, we’ll compare and contrast tuples with structs to build on what you already know and demonstrate when structs are a better way to group data.

keyTerms.definition: In this chapter, we’ll look at enumerations, also referred to as _enums_. Enums allow you to define a type by enumerating its possible variants. First we’ll define and use an enum to show how an enum can encode meaning along with data. Next, we’ll explore a particularly useful enum, called `Option`, which expresses that a value can be either something or nothing. Then, we’ll look at how pattern matching in the `match` expression makes it easy to run different code for different values of an enum. Finally, we’ll cover how the `if let` construct is another convenient and concise idiom available to handle enums in your code.
Reasoning from the concrete or inferred Rust type to valid representation and operations.
Rust expressions such as if, match, and loop direct evaluation and may produce values under their specific rules.

children.text: As you write large programs, organizing your code will become increasingly
important. By grouping related functionality and separating code with distinct
features, you’ll clarify where to find code that implements a particular
feature and where to go to change how a feature works.
The programs we’ve written so far have been in one module in one file. As a
project grows, you should organize code by splitting it into multiple modules
and then multiple files. A package can contain multiple binary crates and
optionally one library crate. As a package grows, you can extract parts into
separate crates that become external dependencies. This chapter covers all
these techniques. For very large projects comprising a set of interrelated
packages that evolve together, Cargo provides workspaces, which we’ll cover in
We’ll also discuss encapsulating implementation details, which lets you reuse
code at a higher level: Once you’ve implemented an operation, other code can
call your code via its public interface without having to know how the
implementation works. The way you write code defines which parts are public for
other code to use and which parts are private implementation details that you
reserve the right to change. This is another way to limit the amount of detail
you have to keep in your head.
A related concept is scope: The nested context in which code is written has a
set of names that are defined as “in scope.” When reading, writing, and
compiling code, programmers and compilers need to know whether a particular
name at a particular spot refers to a variable, function, struct, enum, module,
constant, or other item and what that item means. You can create scopes and
change which names are in or out of scope. You can’t have two items with the
same name in the same scope; tools are available to resolve name conflicts.
Rust has a number of features that allow you to manage your code’s
organization, including which details are exposed, which details are private,
and what names are in each scope in your programs. These features, sometimes
: A Cargo feature that lets you build, test, and share crates
: A tree of modules that produces a library or executable
: Let you control the organization, scope, and privacy of
: A way of naming an item, such as a struct, function, or module
In this chapter, we’ll cover all these features, discuss how they interact, and
explain how to use them to manage scope. By the end, you should have a solid
understanding of the module system and be able to work with scopes like a pro!

keyTerms.definition: Rust’s standard library includes a number of very useful data structures called _collections_. Most other data types represent one specific value, but collections can contain multiple values. Unlike the built-in array and tuple types, the data that these collections point to is stored on the heap, which means the amount of data does not need to be known at compile time and can grow or shrink as the program runs. Each kind of collection has different capabilities and costs, and choosing an appropriate one for your current situation is a skill you’ll develop over time. In this chapter, we’ll discuss three collections that are used very often in Rust programs: - A _vector_ allows you to store a variable number of values next to each other.
A requirements-led choice among sequence, owned UTF-8 text, and key/value lookup structures for the bounded task.
An explicit behavior choice between returning an absence value and panicking on invalid positional access.

children.text: Rust’s standard library includes a number of very useful data structures called
. Most other data types represent one specific value, but
collections can contain multiple values. Unlike the built-in array and tuple
types, the data that these collections point to is stored on the heap, which
means the amount of data does not need to be known at compile time and can grow
or shrink as the program runs. Each kind of collection has different
capabilities and costs, and choosing an appropriate one for your current
situation is a skill you’ll develop over time. In this chapter, we’ll discuss
three collections that are used very often in Rust programs:

Using an Enum to Store Multiple Types
Vectors can only store values that are of the same type. This can be
inconvenient; there are definitely use cases for needing to store a list of
items of different types. Fortunately, the variants of an enum are defined
under the same enum type, so when we need one type to represent elements of
different types, we can define and use an enum!
For example, say we want to get values from a row in a spreadsheet in which
some of the columns in the row contain integers, some floating-point numbers,
and some strings. We can define an enum whose variants will hold the different

at compile time that every possible case is handled, as discussed in Chapter 6.
If you don’t know the exhaustive set of types a program will get at runtime to

Another point about UTF-8 is that there are actually three relevant ways to
look at strings from Rust’s perspective: as bytes, scalar values, and grapheme
clusters (the closest thing to what we would call
If we look at the Hindi word “नमस्ते” written in the Devanagari script, it is

They’re diacritics that don’t make sense on their own. Finally, if we look at
them as grapheme clusters, we’d get what a person would call the four letters
that make up the Hindi word:
Rust provides different ways of interpreting the raw string data that computers
store so that each program can choose the interpretation it needs, no matter
what human language the data is in.
A final reason Rust doesn’t allow us to index into a
character is that indexing operations are expected to always take constant time
(O(1)). But it isn’t possible to guarantee that performance with a
because Rust would have to walk through the contents from the beginning to the
index to determine how many valid characters there were.
Indexing into a string is often a bad idea because it’s not clear what the
return type of the string-indexing operation should be: a byte value, a
character, a grapheme cluster, or a string slice. If you really need to use
indices to create string slices, therefore, Rust asks you to be more specific.

There are two ways to cause a panic in practice: by taking an action that causes our code to panic (such as accessing an array past the end) or by explicitly calling the `panic!` macro. In both cases, we cause a panic in our program. By default, these panics will print a failure message, unwind, clean up the stack, and quit. Via an environment variable, you can also have Rust display the call stack when a panic occurs to make it easier to track down the source of the panic.

keyTerms.term: To panic! or Not to panic!
keyTerms.definition: So, how do you decide when you should call `panic!` and when you should return `Result`? When code panics, there’s no way to recover. You could call `panic!` for any error situation, whether there’s a possible way to recover or not, but then you’re making the decision that a situation is unrecoverable on behalf of the calling code. When you choose to return a `Result` value, you give the calling code options. The calling code could choose to attempt to recover in a way that’s appropriate for its situation, or it could decide that an `Err` value in this case is unrecoverable, so it can call `panic!`

type in each instance, we pay no runtime cost for using generics. When the code
runs, it performs just as it would if we had duplicated each definition by
hand. The process of monomorphization makes Rust’s generics extremely efficient

that every reference in Rust has a lifetime, which is the scope for which

keyTerms.definition: Just as `cargo run` compiles your code and then runs the resultant binary, `cargo test` compiles your code in test mode and runs the resultant test binary. The default behavior of the binary produced by `cargo test` is to run all the tests in parallel and capture output generated during test runs, preventing the output from being displayed and making it easier to read the output related to the test results. You can, however, specify command line options to change this default behavior.

Running Tests in Parallel or Consecutively
When you run multiple tests, by default they run in parallel using threads,
meaning they finish running more quickly and you get feedback sooner. Because
the tests are running at the same time, you must make sure your tests don’t
depend on each other or on any shared state, including a shared environment,
such as the current working directory or environment variables.
For example, say each of your tests runs some code that creates a file on disk
and writes some data to that file. Then, each test
reads the data in that file and asserts that the file contains a particular
value, which is different in each test. Because the tests run at the same time,
one test might overwrite the file in the time between when another test is
writing and reading the file. The second test will then fail, not because the
code is incorrect but because the tests have interfered with each other while
running in parallel. One solution is to make sure each test writes to a
different file; another solution is to run the tests one at a time.
If you don’t want to run the tests in parallel or if you want more fine-grained
control over the number of threads used, you can send the
and the number of threads you want to use to the test binary. Take a look at

The Rust community thinks about tests in terms of two main categories: unit tests and integration tests. _Unit tests_ are small and more focused, testing one module in isolation at a time, and can test private interfaces. _Integration tests_ are entirely external to your library and use your code in the same way any other external code would, using only the public interface and potentially exercising multiple modules per test.
A test compiled within the crate/module context and optimized for local feedback and precise failure localization.
A separate tests/ crate that can reach only public items and therefore verifies consumer-visible contracts.

Rust’s testing features provide a way to specify how code should function to
ensure that it continues to work as you expect, even as you make changes. Unit
tests exercise different parts of a library separately and can test private
implementation details. Integration tests check that many parts of the library
work together correctly, and they use the library’s public API to test the code
in the same way external code will use it. Even though Rust’s type system and
ownership rules help prevent some kinds of bugs, tests are still important to
reduce logic bugs having to do with how your code is expected to behave.

children.text: An I/O Project: Building a Command Line Program
This chapter is a recap of the many skills you’ve learned so far and an
exploration of a few more standard library features. We’ll build a command line
tool that interacts with file and command line input/output to practice some of
the Rust concepts you now have under your belt.
Rust’s speed, safety, single binary output, and cross-platform support make it
an ideal language for creating command line tools, so for our project, we’ll
make our own version of the classic command line search tool
searches a specified file for a specified string. To
takes as its arguments a file path and a string. Then, it reads
the file, finds lines in that file that contain the string argument, and prints
Along the way, we’ll show how to make our command line tool use the terminal
features that many other command line tools use. We’ll read the value of an
environment variable to allow the user to configure the behavior of our tool.
We’ll also print error messages to the standard error console stream (
) so that, for example, the user can
redirect successful output to a file while still seeing error messages onscreen.

keyTerms.definition: To improve our program, we’ll fix four problems that have to do with the program’s structure and how it’s handling potential errors. First, our `main` function now performs two tasks: It parses arguments and reads files. As our program grows, the number of separate tasks the `main` function handles will increase. As a function gains responsibilities, it becomes more difficult to reason about, harder to test, and harder to change without breaking one of its parts. It’s best to separate functionality so that each function is responsible for one task.

design. Writing the test before you write the code that makes the test pass

and output, lifetimes, testing, and command line parsing.

environment variables and how to print to standard error, both of which are
useful when you’re writing command line programs.

from their environment. These closures can be called more than once without

The iterator pattern allows you to perform some task on a sequence of items in
turn. An iterator is responsible for the logic of iterating over each item and
determining when the sequence has finished. When you use iterators, you don’t
have to reimplement that logic yourself.

children.text: To determine whether to use loops or iterators, you need to know which
implementation is faster: the version of the
loop or the version with iterators.
We ran a benchmark by loading the entire contents of
by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle into a
in the contents. Here are the results of the benchmark on the
loop and the version using iterators:

test bench_search_for  ... bench:  19,620,300 ns/iter (+/- 915,700)
test bench_search_iter ... bench:  19,234,900 ns/iter (+/- 657,200)
The two implementations have similar performance! We won’t explain the
benchmark code here because the point is not to prove that the two versions
are equivalent but to get a general sense of how these two implementations
For a more comprehensive benchmark, you should check using various texts of
, different words and words of different lengths
, and all kinds of other variations. The point is this:
Iterators, although a high-level abstraction, get compiled down to roughly the
same code as if you’d written the lower-level code yourself. Iterators are one
, by which we mean that using the abstraction
imposes no additional runtime overhead. This is analogous to how Bjarne
Stroustrup, the original designer and implementor of C++, defines
zero-overhead in his 2012 ETAPS keynote presentation “Foundations of C++”:
In general, C++ implementations obey the zero-overhead principle: What you
don’t use, you don’t pay for. And further: What you do use, you couldn’t hand
In many cases, Rust code using iterators compiles to the same assembly you’d
write by hand. Optimizations such as loop unrolling and eliminating bounds
checking on array access apply and make the resultant code extremely efficient.
Now that you know this, you can use iterators and closures without fear! They
make code seem like it’s higher level but don’t impose a runtime performance
Closures and iterators are Rust features inspired by functional programming
language ideas. They contribute to Rust’s capability to clearly express
high-level ideas at low-level performance. The implementations of closures and
iterators are such that runtime performance is not affected. This is part of
Rust’s goal to strive to provide zero-cost abstractions.
